scores.accuracy_concern: Liu et al. is a small US senior-living sample (93 stick users; Arch Gerontol Geriatr 2011;52:299-303), so 'often wrong' must be presented as that study's finding; the opposite-hand rule applies to one-sided leg problems, and some people need a frame rather than a stick; the ferrule claim still needs an opened source.
scores.sharpen: Lead with the wrist-crease check as a ten-second test the reader can do now, and add one line on when a stick is the wrong aid and a physiotherapist should assess.

scores.accuracy_concern: Restricted activity may mark more serious illness rather than cause decline (confounding by severity), so the opening instruction goes beyond an associational finding and must be marked as judgement; Gill 2004 and 2010 details are unverified.
scores.sharpen: Recast the opening as clearly marked judgement and put the null result in the high-risk group on the visual, so the post reads as careful evidence reading rather than an instruction drawn from an association.

scores.accuracy_concern: LiFE was a three-arm trial (LiFE, structured home exercise, gentle-exercise control); the structured arm was also home-based and its falls reduction was not statistically significant, so the trial did not compare home with class-based training; results apply to people with recent falls and without moderate to severe cognitive impairment. Falls outcome also overlaps category C01.
scores.sharpen: Name the three arms honestly and reframe the angle around training built into daily routines rather than 'without a class', with one concrete LiFE move pictured.

scores.accuracy_concern: No evidence that bringing the person's own frame changes outcomes; ward teams often assess and supply a different aid, and personal aids can go missing; ambulance policy on carrying frames is unverified and varies between services.
scores.sharpen: Fold the walking aid into a broader 'what to bring to hospital' item or merge with C02-17, and drop the ambulance claim unless a service policy can be sourced.

scores.values_concern: Crossing timings are a policy question: keep to reporting the study authors' recommendation and do not imply Alasdair's own policy position.
scores.accuracy_concern: The 1.2 m/s figure is background from the paper's introduction and needs a current Department for Transport source; HSE walking speed was timed over a short course (about 8 feet) from a standing start, which may understate speed on a crossing; data are from 2005; many UK crossings with detectors (Puffin) extend clearance time, so 'timed for' needs qualification.
scores.sharpen: Put the test method and survey year on the chart and add one line on crossings with detectors, so the striking comparison stays accurate.

scores.accuracy_concern: The hazard ratio of 0.88 per 0.1 m/s is a population association; the 19% to 87% survival range spans the extremes of gait speed and must not be read as an individual prediction; the list of causes of slow gait still needs a source; cohorts were 1986 to 2000 and about 80% white.
scores.sharpen: Open with the Studenski survival range at age 75 as the visual hook, then turn at once to what to do for one slow patient: measure, repeat, look for causes.

scores.accuracy_concern: ASCOF measure numbering and wording changed in the 2023 to 2024 refresh and must be checked; ASCOF also reports an outcome-of-short-term-services measure, which is not a function measure but should be acknowledged; the measure covers England only and the handbook is an official web document that may not be openable here.
scores.sharpen: Name one concrete alternative (a function score or goal attainment at the end of reablement) so the criticism ends with something services could adopt.

scores.values_concern: Avoid implying that therapists or ward teams are risk-averse as a group; frame the problem as the question and the note format, not the profession.
scores.accuracy_concern: Section 1(4) of the Mental Capacity Act applies only when the person has capacity for that decision, so the post must say what happens when capacity is lacking (best interests, least restrictive option); the risk-aversion qualitative claim still needs a source; the 2007 DH guidance may be superseded. Category fit is partly C09 or C15.
scores.sharpen: Lead with the four-line note structure as the visual and add one sentence on best-interests decisions when the person lacks capacity for this decision.

scores.accuracy_concern: Sinoff and Ore 1997 compared self-reported with observed Barthel performance in the old-old and reported discrepancies (self-report tending to overstate ability, particularly with cognitive impairment), which cuts against the claim that self-report is reasonably consistent; the documentation-gap claim has no source yet.
scores.sharpen: Drop the self-report validity claim and keep it as a clerking teaching card built around the six questions and the reason 'independently mobile' gives rehabilitation no target.

scores.accuracy_concern: Loyd 2020's pooled 30% combines studies using pre-admission and admission baselines; the first-hour task list is a judgement, not a tested checklist; the NICE NG27 wording on home assessment is unverified.
scores.sharpen: Cut the list to five tasks that read at phone size and add who to ask (the ward therapist) and what to request if a task has not been tried.

scores.accuracy_concern: Direct evidence that each attachment reduces mobility in older inpatients is limited (the catheter 'one-point restraint' source is an editorial); the idle-cannula prevalence needs a checked source; oxygen and monitoring decisions are clinical, so families can ask but staff decide.
scores.sharpen: Build it around one daily question ('Which of these still needs to be here today?') and source the idle-cannula figure before using it.

scores.values_concern: The 41.3% who died within a year is a stark figure for a family audience; present it with context and without drama.
scores.accuracy_concern: Boyd's cohort is US data from 1993 to 1998; the one-month finding is prognostic and does not show that a review at one month improves outcomes; check that Hardy and Gill's 81% refers to recovery from an episode of disability and that recovery was often not sustained.
scores.sharpen: Lead with the recovery range, mark the one-month review as judgement, and give families the specific request (a review of walking and daily activities around four weeks after discharge).

scores.values_concern: Avoid reading as blame of ward staff; aim the criticism at what is measured.
scores.accuracy_concern: The claim that functional loss is not a routine UK harm indicator is an absence claim that needs a checkable source or softening; Loyd's pooled figure mixes baselines; the 'little change over time' finding needs checking in full text. Shares the Loyd statistic with C02-10.
scores.sharpen: Pair the 3 in 10 figure with one named, simple measure a ward could start recording, and soften the national-indicator claim to what can be verified.

scores.values_concern: Keep the framing on time, training and rota design so care workers are not blamed for doing tasks for people.
scores.accuracy_concern: The Baltes studies date from the 1980s and early 1990s in German institutions with small samples and short follow-up; present them as a described pattern and a tested staff programme, not as current UK care home practice; Resnick function-focused care citations are unverified.
scores.sharpen: Date the research in the caption and state the time cost on the rota explicitly, so the post reads as a classic, still-useful finding with a practical implication.

scores.accuracy_concern: Buchner 1996 is cross-sectional, so the claim that small strength changes produce larger walking changes in weak people is inferred from a curve, not observed within people; Kortebein studied healthy older adults; some trials in frail people after hospital showed limited functional gains, so 'large gains' needs qualifying; the 113% is a relative change from a very low baseline.
scores.sharpen: Keep the curve as a labelled illustrative shape and add one line on trials where frail people gained less, so the teaching point does not overpromise.

scores.accuracy_concern: Keep between-group differences (SPPB 2.2, Barthel 6.9) separate from within-group changes (usual care minus 5.0, exercise plus 1.9); single-centre, single-blind, outcomes at discharge only; participants had to be able to walk and cooperate; confirm session length and staffing in full text.
scores.sharpen: Lead with the diverging bars (usual care down, exercise up) and describe what the two daily sessions involved in one plain sentence.

scores.values_concern: Some patients should not walk unaided; frame the family question around today's plan rather than pressure to walk.
scores.accuracy_concern: Brown 2009 was 45 older male veterans in one US hospital; generalising the 83% figure to UK wards needs a second source (for example Pedersen 2013, Danish medical inpatients); the '78% willing and able' figure should be checked against the abstract.
scores.sharpen: Add a second, non-veteran source for time in bed and phrase the question as 'What is the walking plan for today?' so it prompts a plan rather than a demand.

scores.accuracy_concern: EWGSOP2 cut-offs are European and differ from the Asian (AWGS 2019) criteria; the 2024 GLIS definition is conceptual and gives no operational cut-offs, so mixing it into the pathway may confuse; the 'no licensed medicine' claim needs a BNF or MHRA check.
scores.sharpen: Add one practical starting point for resistance exercise and one line on what to tell the patient, so the post goes beyond the diagnostic pathway to action.

scores.values_concern: Avoid implying care home staff neglect residents; aim the point at low expectations and access to therapy.
scores.accuracy_concern: The 113% strength gain is a relative change from a low baseline, achieved with supervised high-intensity machine training in residents able to take part; data are from 1994; the Cochrane review found smaller and less certain effects; the UK physiotherapy-access claim has no source yet. Shares the Fiatarone trial with C02-15 and C02-29.
scores.sharpen: State that the training was supervised and high intensity on resistance machines, and put the more modest Cochrane picture in the caption rather than only a footnote.

scores.accuracy_concern: The proportion meeting the strength guideline is unverified; the post must not imply walking has little value; the CMO documents are gov.uk pages that may not open here, so a published summary of the guideline is needed.
scores.sharpen: Open with one concrete strength activity from the CMO infographic and a sourced figure for how few older adults meet the strength guideline.

scores.accuracy_concern: Most implicit motor-learning evidence comes from laboratory tasks in mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease; transfer to real rehabilitation tasks and to other dementias is less certain; the exclusion-from-rehabilitation claim needs a source; Hauer 2012 details to verify.
scores.sharpen: Show one concrete demonstration-based technique (the same sit-to-stand sequence with one cue each time) and state that the evidence is mainly in Alzheimer's disease.

scores.accuracy_concern: The sequence assumes the person can bear weight and follow instructions; people who cannot need an assessment and equipment; the 'drag lift is unsafe' claim needs an openable moving and handling source; some guidance allows a palm-to-palm hand hold, so avoid an absolute ban on any hand contact.
scores.sharpen: Add a final panel on when to stop and ask for an assessment or equipment (cannot take weight, dizzy, knees buckle), sourced to moving and handling guidance.

scores.accuracy_concern: Brown 2016 was 100 US veterans (97% male) at one centre; check that life-space was a pre-specified main outcome, otherwise 'the choice of measure decided' reads as outcome selection; the life-space associations with death and care home admission need primary sources. Shares the Brown 2016 trial with C02-17.
scores.sharpen: Lead with the concentric-zone diagram and give readers a plain question they can use ('How far from your front door did you get last month?').

scores.accuracy_concern: Carli 2020 compared prehabilitation with the same programme started after surgery, not with no programme; 110 patients may be underpowered for complications; check the umbrella review's certainty ratings exactly, especially for functional recovery; confirm the PREHAB (McIsaac 2022) result before citing it. Category fit is partly C07.
scores.sharpen: State plainly that the comparison was prehabilitation versus the same programme after surgery, and end with the counselling sentence practitioners can use.

scores.values_concern: Risks presenting family practice as an expectation and shifting therapy work onto unpaid relatives; the choice must be explicit and safety central.
scores.accuracy_concern: Extra therapy delivered by therapists does not show that family-led practice gives the same benefit; the family-exercise trial (FAME) is in stroke; there is no evidence cited on the safety of family-assisted walking in older inpatients.
scores.sharpen: Centre the post on the safety question ('What should I not do, and when do I call a nurse?') or merge it with C02-17 as a single family-facing hospital mobility post.

scores.accuracy_concern: Gerlach 2012 is self-reported survey data and Gerlach 2013 is a small cohort (46 admissions), so 'none who self-managed deteriorated' rests on small numbers; confirm NICE NG71 wording and recommendation number; overlaps medicine-timing territory in C06.
scores.sharpen: Lead with the concrete admission request (self-administration or doses at the person's usual times) and describe the survey findings as self-reported.

scores.accuracy_concern: Peak plasma concentration is not the same as peak analgesic effect; regular paracetamol makes timing less relevant, so the point applies mainly to as-needed doses; opioid sedation and dizziness before mobilisation need mention; NICE CG124 wording to verify.
scores.sharpen: Focus on as-needed opioid doses before therapy, add the sedation and dizziness caution, and use sourced onset times on the timeline.

scores.values_concern: A critique of a well-meant campaign with named originators; keep it fair and avoid implying staff are not trying.
scores.accuracy_concern: One small Canadian quality improvement project's 14% cannot stand for the campaign; the Alberta time-series study reported falls in length of stay and inpatient falls, which must be stated as plainly; the 'no randomised trial' claim needs a documented search; 70-day challenge dates unverified.
scores.sharpen: Report the favourable Alberta findings as plainly as the shortfall, and give practitioners one simple measure (the proportion of patients up and dressed by midday).

scores.values_concern: Avoid implying families wasted money or made a poor choice; offer a better use of effort.
scores.accuracy_concern: In Fiatarone 1994 the supplemented residents reduced their usual food intake, so total intake rose little; the trial does not show supplements are ineffective in general, and its population (frail nursing home residents) differs from community families; protein target figures and the Liao meta-analysis need checking.
scores.sharpen: Mention the substitution effect in the Fiatarone trial and base the advice on the guideline ranking (exercise first, protein as support) rather than on that single trial.

allocation_reason: Twenty-eight of 29 candidates reach 36 with no disqualifying flag and 18 score 42 or more across distinct angles (sarcopenia diagnosis, rehabilitation in dementia, walking aids, sit-to-stand, crossing times, in-hospital exercise, prehabilitation, life-space, Parkinson's medicine timing), so the category supports the maximum even after clustered near-duplicates are thinned.
balance_note: The top 14 by score are practitioner-heavy: 7 practitioners (C02-21, 18, 24, 16, 08, 15, 27), 4 both (C02-14, 05, 23, 26) and 3 public (C02-01, 10, 22). To give older people and carers substantial coverage, swap C02-15 for C02-19 (public; shares the Fiatarone trial, so take only one of 15, 19 and 29) and consider C02-03 or C02-17 (public) in place of C02-27. Thin the clusters: hospital mobility (C02-16, 17, 11, 28, 04: take at most two), post-discharge function (C02-10, 12, 13, 07: at most two, and C02-10 and C02-13 share the Loyd figure), walking speed (C02-05 and 06 make different points and can both stand). The top set mixes good care and teaching (C02-14, 16, 18, 21, 22) with evidence-based criticism (C02-05, 23, 24), which fits the category's 'practical and hopeful as well as critical' brief.
